Here comes a little update from the Finland “Species” project fieldwork from 2026 spring/summer

The Rovaniemi “Species” team Florian Stammler, Heidi Konttinen, Aytalina Ivanova, Nuccio Mazullo have started fieldwork in a multi-species approach in two different sites. We focus on one of them here, the marine one, and the relations between people, seals, salmon and the sea.

We spent some fascinating time in the small port of Ajos, Finland’s northernmost Sea port. This is the perfect place to develop an understanding of people’s relations with fish and seals, as it is the same families who engage in both fishing and seal hunting. This was historically the case, before outsiders established legislation that separated these two species and stigmatised human-seal relations.

What seems to be a conflict between two species (salmon and seal) at first glance turned out to be two sides of an intimate way of knowing the sea and its inhabitants. Of course no one denies that seals eat fish. And since nothing from seals can be sold in Finland (due to the EU ban), fish is the species that keeps the little port in Ajos running. So yes, people take various measures preventing seals to eat the fish from their nets.

Going out for salmon fishing with two of our hosts there was a memorable experience. The first unusual setting is that we fish salmon in the sea , and not in the river. Secondly, this is done with very inventive high-tech: the fishers install huge fish-traps on inflatable runners (see pic salmon_trap_dry), and place them in the right place not far off the coast (see pic salmontrap_water). Each of those has of course their own registration number. The price of one of these fish traps is tremendous, many 1000 Euros! They leave the traps for a day or two in the water, and then sail out to check them. A compressor in the boat can inflate the runners on the bottom of the traps, and they raise above the water level, from where the fisher can retrieve the catch (see salmontrap_raise, salmontrap_raised_up).

We are wondering where this weird noise, some constant whistling comes from. Our host points to little black round boxes floating close to the fish traps. They emit this noise at a studied frequency that make it uncomfortable for seals to approach the fish traps. These boxes are Acoustic Deterrent Devices (ADD) for seals (see pic salmon_in_net_seal_deterrant_in_background_marked, Seal_acoustic_deterrent_copyright_LUKE).

Each of these boxes also costs 13000s of Euros, but part of that sum is funded by the government for professional fishers. The noise is at a frequency that makes it less likely for seals to want to spend much time in the vicinity of these boxes. Our host tells us that some animal activists are worried about the impact that these boxes have on the seals’ wellbeing. However, still some fish have traces of contact with seals, as we witness ourselves (see pic salmon_injured_by_seal). We conceive of this rather as an example of how people, seals and fish negotiate the terms and conditions of their relations: the deterrent devices are signs for seals where they should leave some fish-food for people, during the very short salmon fishing season in the area. Fishers are also seal hunters. Actually their ancestors are bearers of the old Bothnian Bay sealing culture that external pressures have driven close to disappearing. So by no way do these people want to do harm to the seals. The boxes are thus another means of communicating with the seals – telling them that these particular places are for people to catch salmon, while the seals are welcome to catch them somewhere else, not necessarily in people’s traps.
The traps are also made in a way that seals will not end up entangled in the meshwork and die. So a lot of measures are in place to negotiate people-seal-fish relations on the technical side.

Hence, at the end of this fishing part of the fieldwork we understand how technology turns what may seem a sustainability conflict at first glance, into a triangle relationship between three species (people, fish and salmon). Doing anthropological fieldwork like this is not just about interviewing people. It is about taking part, using your own body as a fieldwork tool, and in doing so learning to also physically engage with the Species in focus. We are therefore especially thankful to the sealers and fishers to have been so patient and teach us. This leads also to an entirely different level of conversation. On the boat we witness how the law is omnipresent in this operation: each fish has to be marked (see pic salmon_marking , salmon_marking_closeup , salmon_processed_marked ). During the joint filetting of the salmon, we find out that at the height of the season – midsummer – most of the calmon are filled with caviar, but which is so small that is has no market value. However, privately fishers can still use it, although they will not always have time to wash, salt and freeze it. Part of our “making” (Ingold 2013) approach is that we do so ourselves, with a delicious result! (see pic Florian_Stammler_Caviar_packaging, caviar&salted_ready). One important tradition among the salmon fishers of Ajos is the midsummer festive meal consisting of salmon heads (see pic Salmon_head_traditional_midsummer_meal). The heads will not go on sale, so fishers grill them on very hot charcoal, making for a delicious meal at midsummer (see pic Salmon_head_traditional_midsummer_meal_grill) , an important yearly holiday in all Nordic countries.

While salmon fishing season is just around midsummer, the season for the Bay of Bothnia traditional seal hunt is from mid-April for approximately a month. The season used to start much earlier, when people went out to the sea ice for hunting as early as February. But again – some external actors decided to make the hunt illegal before mid April, which caused trouble for the local livelihood: by late spring time, people fix their fishing gear and prepare for the fishing season, and would not necessarily spend their time for seal hunting any more. Moreover, the ice gets thinner, or is further away from the shore, driving up the costs for the seal hunt.

But we end up going on the May holiday, the 30th April / 1st May. In a 14 hour trip we get one seal, and get the feeling how important this activity is the for hunters emotionally, culturally and for their identity rather than economically: there is no income possible from the seals, and the gear and fuel cost a fortune, so only people with good other jobs can afford to hunt these days (see pic Petrol_costs) . What is different about this particular seal hunt is both the species and the method: here we deal with the special Baltic ringed seal, Pusa hispida botnica,  which is allowed to hunt only in the Bothnian Bay and the Kvarken Archipelago in the northern Baltic Sea. And the traditional way in which it is done includes a very specific material culture that has evolved over the centuries, which is hard to keep alive when it becomes such an expensive hobby. Hunting is done only on the ice (see pic sealhunt_inspection), for example using a specially designed monoski called “ajopuu”, (see pic Ajopuu_sealing_tool) when seals rest in the spring sun on the ice, or rise through their breathing holes.

Our team headed by Heidi Konttinen together with the seal hunters association had tried to bring this seal hunting culture on to the list of intangible cultural heritage in Finland – but we were refused, maybe due to the difficult political tensions around seal hunting connected to the EU ban, animal welfare and international campaigns. Still we find it somehow ambiguous that in Finland they import seal skins from South Greenland, where the Great Greenland sealskin tannery (see separately attached IMG_3567) is exempt from the EU ban, and then they produce nice sealskin products to sell in Finland, while on the other hand they do so much for preventing the old Bay of Bothnia sealing culture in our own country to thrive again.

So part of our work in the species project is to document the multiple ways of hunters engaging with the seal (see pic Multimodal_fieldwork), and making things of it. The hunt itself has an almost solemn atmosphere to it when we have finally found the right spot, after so many hours of searching in the already way too open water. From the distance we observe silently how the hunter approaches carefully the breathing hole, hides behind a pice of ice (see pic sealhunt_creeping_to_shoot_position). We find out that identifying the right place is to shoot is by far not only about the best position for making a good shot (see pic sealhunt_shooting). As important is the relational aspect: a good shooting place is one where the terrain between seal and hunter is easily enough to move through for retrieving the seal quickly after that shot (see pic  seal_retrieved). Because one important moral code of conduct is that you must not shoot before you are convinced you have good chances to recover the seal. On the evening of the hunt we can document the butchering of the meat (see pic seal_butchering, seal_butchered), while the next day goes to the handling of the skin and fat. This is Heidi Konttinen’s specific focus for her PhD, so we won’t write too much of this here (see pic Heidi sealskin_clean_karcher).

One little known use of the seal fat is as an additive for house paint. Traditionally, the fat was cooked and mixed with the traditional red house paint made with clay pigments (see pic sealfat_cooking). In the coastal villages, the seal fat additive made this paint extremely weather resistant, while at the same time allowing the wood to breathe. Our host tells us that to this day churches in the sealing villages of the Bay of Bothnia  are painted with this, which has kept historical buildings in better shape than any other industrially produced paint. Some private customers still order such hand-made high-quality paint for their houses from seal hunters there. On the 1st of May, we make some additional effort for cleaning the fat of any meat residue before cooking, which allows us to get pure precious seal oil full of healthy omega+3 acids. The technology is the same as for producing the paint-additive: through cooking the solid part of the fat gets separated from the liquid, and you get a clear oil (see pic sealfat_Omega3_separation). The oil of seals is actually supposed to be better digestible for people than that of fish, which is usually sold over the counter. The reason is very species relational: both humans and seals are mammal, so their fat is more similar to each other, hence we digest sealfat omega oil more easily than fish omega oil. The Greenlanders got it right in their tradition of eating seal blubber, which is probably why we have not seen them preparing such seal oil from their seals. Eating the frozen or fresh blubber gives enough of the omega 3 to people. In Europe this is so uncommon that people prefer to buy the ingredients in the pharmacy…
Hence, the fieldwork in this project continues to give us surprising insights we would not have thought of before.
